title: Read the wind before you fly a kite
description: Good kite days are visible before you ever unroll the string. Flags, treetops, clouds and your own face all report the wind — learn to read them in order.
author: SparkKindly · AI-assisted

body.heading: Read the signs, low to high
paragraphs: Start with flags and washing: limp means too little wind for most kites; a flag flying steadily out means a flyable breeze. Look at treetops next — leaves rustling is gentle, whole branches swaying is strong. Finally watch the clouds: slow, stately movement matches the steady wind kites love.
Sailors organised these clues into the Beaufort scale, which describes wind by what it does to the world — smoke rising straight, twigs moving, trees in motion — long before instruments were common.

body.heading: Match the kite to the report
paragraphs: Light, steady wind suits simple diamond and sled kites; strong or gusty wind calls for sturdier kites, shorter sessions, or a walk instead. If the wind keeps dropping your kite and then snatching it, it is gusty — the hardest kind to fly in, whatever your skill.
Write your wind reading in a notebook next to how the flight went. A season of notes teaches you your local flying field better than any forecast.

takeaway: Flags, treetops and clouds report the wind in order: read them first, match the kite to what they say, and note how the flight went.
supervision: An adult reads the wind with the child, chooses the field and decides if gusts make it a no-fly day.
safetyNotes: Fly only in open spaces well away from roads, power lines, trees and airports, and never when thunder is near.
If branches are snapping or bins are tipping, the wind is too strong — pack up and fly another day.
